lead: A ball thrown at a wall taller than its energy always comes back. An electron does not. When its energy E is less than a barrier height V, its wavefunction still leaks into the barrier, decays exponentially across width a, and leaves a small amplitude on the far side. That is quantum tunnelling. Transmission falls exponentially with width, so a gap a few atoms wide can switch a large current. Tunnelling explains alpha decay, the tunnel diode, the scanning tunnelling microscope, and the fusion reactions that power the Sun.
prereq: You need: 6.7 The Schrodinger equation, 6.6 The wavefunction and Born's interpretation, 6.8 Particle in a box, and ordinary exponential decay.

sections.h3: A barrier the particle cannot climb

blocks.text: A particle of mass m moves along x with total energy E. At x = 0 it meets a rectangular barrier: potential energy V for 0 < x < a and zero outside. V and E are in joules, a is the barrier width in metres. Inside the barrier the kinetic energy would be E − V.

Classical mechanics stops here. If E < V then E − V is negative, kinetic energy cannot be negative, so the particle must turn back. Reflection probability is 1 and transmission is 0. A cricket ball thrown at a concrete wall obeys this.

Quantum mechanics does not stop here. The particle is a wavefunction ψ, and |ψ|² is a probability density (see 6.6). A wave meeting a change of potential is partly reflected and partly transmitted, as light is at glass. So there is a non-zero probability of detecting the particle beyond x = a even when E < V.

Nothing is climbed, and energy is conserved. The particle never possesses negative kinetic energy at any measured instant. It appears on the far side with the same energy E it started with, because a single particle cannot be caught halfway.
Start from the time-independent Schrodinger equation for a constant potential.

blocks.where: ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; m is mass in kg; ψ(x) is the wavefunction; V barrier height in J; E total energy in J.

blocks.text: Inside the barrier V > E, so (E − V) is negative. Rearranging gives d²ψ/dx² = κ²ψ with κ real and positive.

blocks.where: κ decay constant in m⁻¹; V − E barrier excess in J; m mass in kg; ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

blocks.text: The coefficient of ψ is positive, so solutions are e^(+κx) and e^(−κx), not sines and cosines. For a wide barrier the growing term is unphysical, leaving ψ(x) = A e^(−κx): the wave shrinks smoothly instead of oscillating.
The amplitude at x = a is smaller than at x = 0 by e^(−κa). The probability is the square.

blocks.where: T transmission probability (0 to 1); κ in m⁻¹; a width in m.

blocks.text: The standard thick-barrier result, good to leading order when κa ≫ 1, is T = 16E(V − E)/V² × e^(−2κa). The prefactor can be dropped only when E is far from V/2 or κa is very large, say κa > 5.

items: T is exponentially sensitive to a: doubling the width squares T.
T falls as √(V − E) grows, because κ grows that way.
A finite well shows the same mathematics: outside a well of finite depth the wavefunction decays as e^(−κx). The particle is partly found outside the well.

blocks.text: Alpha decay. An alpha particle inside a heavy nucleus is held by the strong force but pushed out by the Coulomb barrier of the protons. Its energy is far below that barrier, yet it escapes by tunnelling. Because T is exponential in energy, a small change in alpha energy changes the half-life by many powers of ten (Geiger–Nuttall relation).

Tunnel diode. A p-n junction (Unit 7, Metal-semiconductor junctions) is doped so heavily that the depletion layer is only a few nanometres wide. Electrons tunnel straight across it. The current-voltage curve has a region where current falls as voltage rises; this negative resistance makes the diode useful in high-frequency oscillators.

Scanning tunnelling microscope. A sharp metal tip is held a fraction of a nanometre above a conducting surface, with vacuum as the barrier. Electrons tunnel across and give a measurable current. A 0.1 nm change in gap changes current by about one order of magnitude, giving atomic-resolution images. Flash memory uses the same effect: electrons tunnel through a thin oxide layer onto a floating gate.

Nuclear fusion in the Sun. Protons in the solar core have thermal energies of a few keV, while their mutual Coulomb barrier is around an MeV. Without tunnelling, two protons could never fuse. The tiny transmission probability is enough, because the core holds an enormous number of protons.

figure.caption: An electron of energy 1.0 eV meets a 2.0 eV barrier of width 0.5 nm. The wavefunction decays inside with κ = 5.12 × 10⁹ m⁻¹ and emerges with small amplitude. The simple form gives T ≈ 0.60 % (about 2.4 % with the prefactor).

spec.title: Tunnelling through a barrier
spec.aria: An incident electron of energy 1.0 eV hits a barrier of height 2.0 eV and width 0.5 nm, decays exponentially inside with kappa 5.12 times 10 to the 9 per metre, exits with small amplitude, and gives simple-form transmission about 0.60 percent, about 2.4 percent with the prefactor.

examples.question: An electron of energy E = 1.0 eV faces a rectangular barrier of height V = 2.0 eV and width a = 0.5 nm. Using T ≈ e^(−2κa) with κ = √(2m(V − E))/ℏ, find κ, 2κa, and T. Take ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
steps: Convert energies to joules: V = 3.204 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, E = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so V − E = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
√(2m(V − E)) = 5.40 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s. This is ℏκ, the magnitude of the imaginary momentum inside the barrier — the momentum a free particle with kinetic energy V − E would carry.

Prefactor: 16E(V − E)/V² = 16 × 1.0 × 1.0 / 2.0² = 4. Fuller formula: T ≈ 4 × 5.98 × 10⁻³ ≈ 2.4 %, four times the simple estimate. They agree only to a factor of a few here. Drop the prefactor only when E is far from V/2 or κa > 5.
examples.answer: κ = 5.12 × 10⁹ m⁻¹, 2κa = 5.12. Simple form T ≈ 6.0 × 10⁻³ (0.60 %); fuller formula T ≈ 2.4 %.
examples.check:
import math
E = 1.0 * 1.602e-19
V = 2.0 * 1.602e-19
m = 9.11e-31
hbar = 1.055e-34
a = 0.5e-9
kappa = math.sqrt(2 * m * (V - E)) / hbar
exponent = 2 * kappa * a
T = math.exp(-exponent)
print(round(kappa / 1e9, 2))
print(round(exponent, 2))
print(round(T, 4))

traps: Using T ≈ e^(−2κa) when κa is not large, e.g. a thin barrier or E close to V; the prefactor 16E(V − E)/V² then matters.
Putting eV numbers into the square root instead of joules changes 2m(V − E) by about 10¹⁹, making κ wrong by about 10⁹–10¹⁰. Convert to joules first.
Writing κa instead of 2κa. Amplitude decays once across the width; probability decays twice.
Claiming negative kinetic energy inside the barrier. ψ decays there; no kinetic energy is measured inside.
Assuming T = 1 when E > V. A particle above a barrier is still partly reflected in general; T = 1 only when E ≫ V, or at resonance energies where the width holds a whole number of half-wavelengths.

quiz.q: Define κ for a rectangular barrier and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: κ = √(2m(V − E))/ℏ, with m in kg, V − E in J, ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Unit: m⁻¹.

quiz.q: A particle with E < V appears beyond a barrier of width a. Why does this not violate energy conservation?
quiz.a: The particle is never observed inside with negative kinetic energy. Its wavefunction decays there, and any detection finds it reflected or transmitted with the same energy E. Only probabilities are spread; energy is fixed.

quiz.q: An electron with E = 1.0 eV meets a barrier of height V = 2.0 eV (κ = 5.12 × 10⁹ m⁻¹) and has T = 6.0 × 10⁻³ at a = 0.5 nm. Find T when the width is doubled to 1.0 nm.
quiz.a: New exponent 2κa = 10.24, so T = e^(−10.24) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁵, the square of the old T.

quiz.q: In a scanning tunnelling microscope the barrier is the vacuum gap and κ = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ m⁻¹. The tip moves 0.1 nm further from the surface. By what factor does the tunnelling current change?
quiz.a: Current ∝ e^(−2κa). Change in exponent: 2 × 1.0 × 10¹⁰ × 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 2. Current falls by e² ≈ 7.4, roughly one order of magnitude. This is why the STM resolves single atoms.

quiz.q: Why does a particle in a finite well have non-zero probability outside the well?
quiz.a: Outside the well the potential exceeds the particle energy, so ψ does not vanish at the wall; it decays as e^(−κx). |ψ|² is small but non-zero just outside and dies away over about 1/κ.

quiz.q: Alpha emitters with slightly larger alpha energy have enormously shorter half-lives. Explain using tunnelling.
quiz.a: The alpha particle tunnels through the Coulomb barrier of the daughter nucleus. Larger E means smaller (V − E), hence smaller κ and much larger e^(−2κa); escape probability rises steeply, so half-life drops by many orders of magnitude for a small energy change.

quiz.q: When is the simplified formula T ≈ e^(−2κa) accurate?
quiz.a: For a thick barrier, κa ≫ 1, so the order-one prefactor 16E(V − E)/V² can be ignored.

beyond: Not for the exam. When the barrier height changes slowly with x, the exponent generalises to an integral of κ(x) over the barrier; this is the WKB approximation. Two barriers in series give resonant tunnelling when the energy matches a quasi-bound state. Thin oxide layers in flash memory and tunnel field-effect transistors use the same exponential. Josephson junctions add a tunnelling supercurrent. Search next for WKB approximation, resonant tunnelling diode, and tunnel field-effect transistor.
